lead: Brazing, soldering and adhesive bonding join parts without melting the parent metal. A filler with a lower melting point wets the surfaces and freezes in the gap; in adhesive bonding the filler is a polymer. Soldering and adhesive bonding run cool enough that the parent metal keeps its strength and heat treatment. Brazing runs hotter, so it avoids melting and distortion of the parent, but its temperature can still temper or anneal some alloys; check the parent's tempering temperature before choosing brazing. These processes allow dissimilar materials to join, and give clean joints. You meet brazed pipe fittings and carbide tool tips, soldered circuit boards, and glued aircraft panels and car trim.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the third joining family and Chapter 4.2 for torch heating.

blocks.text: Brazing joins parts with a filler metal that melts above 450 °C but below the melting point of the parent metal. The parent stays solid. The filler is drawn into a narrow gap by capillary action, the same effect that pulls water up a thin tube. A typical gap is 0.03 mm to 0.2 mm. The joint is designed as a lap, so load is carried in shear over an overlap area, not across a butt line.

blocks.where: h is the capillary rise (m); γ is the filler surface tension (N/m); θ is the contact angle; ρ is the filler density (kg/m³); g = 9.81 m/s²; d is the gap (m).

blocks.text: Before heating, a flux such as borax or a fluoride mixture is applied. The flux dissolves oxide on the metal and protects the clean surface from air, so the filler can wet it. Heating can be by torch, furnace, induction, dip or resistance. The heat source only raises the joint to the filler flow temperature; it does not melt the parent.

Common fillers are silver-based alloys for strong joints at moderate temperature, and copper-zinc (brass) fillers for steel and cast iron. A brazed joint is usually stronger than a soldered joint and can serve at higher temperature, but it is not as strong as a welded joint of the same parent metal. Brazing is used for pipe fittings, heat exchangers, carbide tool tips, bicycle frames and repair of castings. It suits dissimilar metals because the parent never enters the melt.

Soldering uses a filler that melts below 450 °C. The classic tin-lead eutectic (63% Sn, 37% Pb) melts at 183 °C; lead-free alloys commonly melt around 217 °C to 230 °C. The parent metal stays solid, so the joint is a thin layer of solder between the parts. Rosin flux removes oxide and helps wetting.

Hand soldering uses an iron; mass production uses wave soldering for through-hole boards and reflow soldering for surface-mount boards, where solder paste is printed and the board is heated. Because the filler melts below 450 °C, the parent keeps its heat treatment and does not warp as in welding. The joint must be mechanically supported because solder is soft and creeps under load. It cannot be used near high temperature: a soldered joint may fail if it gets hot enough to soften. Soldering is standard in electronics because it makes electrical contact and a modest mechanical joint at low temperature, without damaging components.

sections.h3: Adhesive bonding: a polymer layer joins the parts

blocks.text: Adhesive bonding joins parts with a polymer layer. No metal filler melts. The joint holds by mechanisms quoted as mechanical interlocking (adhesive keying into a rough surface), adsorption (molecular attraction at the interface) and diffusion (polymer chains crossing a compatible interface). Surface preparation is decisive: clean, degrease, abrade or etch, and use a primer where specified.

Design the joint for lap shear, so the adhesive layer is loaded along the overlap, not peeled apart. Adhesives join thin sheets without rivet holes, dissimilar metals without galvanic contact, and composites without drilling fibres. Limits are low service temperature, creep under steady load, and ageing from moisture, ultraviolet light and salt. Adhesive bonds need a controlled gap and often a jig until the polymer cures. They are used for car trim, aircraft panels, electronic potting and repair of thin sheets where welding would distort.
The 450 °C line separates brazing from soldering. In all three lower-temperature processes the parent metal is never melted; only the filler or adhesive changes state.

Choose brazing when the joint needs medium to high strength and must survive above solder temperature, as for pipe fittings and carbide tips. Choose soldering for electrical contact and low-temperature assembly, as on circuit boards. Choose adhesive bonding for thin sheets, dissimilar materials or composites where holes and welding heat are unwanted. The table keeps the four routes separate.

figure.caption: Joining methods from hotter at the top to cooler at the bottom. The parent metal melts only in welding; brazing and soldering melt only a filler, and adhesive bonding uses a polymer.

examples.question: A brazed lap joint has parallel plates separated by d = 0.05 mm. The filler has surface tension γ = 0.9 N/m, contact angle θ = 30°, and density ρ = 8000 kg/m³. Molten brazing fillers are usually near 0.8–1.0 N/m; 0.9 N/m is a typical value here. Estimate the capillary rise h using h = 2γcosθ/(ρgd). Then explain why a real brazed joint fills only a few millimetres, not the estimated height.
steps: Convert the gap: d = 0.05 mm = 0.05 × 10⁻³ m = 5 × 10⁻⁵ m.

h here is the equivalent head 2γcosθ/(ρgd); for a vertical gap it is the rise. In a real lap joint gravity is not the limit — viscous drag of the melt in the narrow gap, trapped air, oxide and freezing on cold metal stop the flow after a few millimetres. Keep the clearance small but not zero, and use a flux.
examples.answer: The estimated equivalent head is 0.3972 m (about 397 mm). In a real lap joint gravity is not the limit: viscous drag of the melt in the narrow gap, trapped air, oxide blocking wetting and freezing on cold metal stop the flow after a few millimetres.
examples.check:
import math
gamma = 0.9
theta = math.radians(30)
rho = 8000
g = 9.81
d = 0.05e-3
num = 2 * gamma * math.cos(theta)
den = rho * g * d
h = num / den
print(f'{h:.4f}')
print(f'{h * 1000:.0f}')

traps: Saying brazing or soldering melts the parent metal. Only the filler melts; the parent stays solid.
Forgetting the 450 °C line. A filler melting above 450 °C is brazing; below 450 °C is soldering.
Using a soldered joint where a brazed joint is needed for load or temperature. Solder is soft and low melting.
Setting the brazing gap to zero for maximum contact. Zero gap leaves no room for filler; too large a gap weakens capillary action. Stay near 0.03–0.2 mm.
Treating flux as optional on a clean-looking surface. Oxide is thin and invisible; flux is still needed to let the filler wet the metal.

quiz.q: State the melting-point boundary that separates brazing from soldering.
quiz.a: Brazing filler melts above 450 °C; soldering filler melts below 450 °C.

quiz.q: Why can brazing join two dissimilar metals without melting either parent?
quiz.a: Only the lower-melting filler melts and wets both solids. The parents do not mix in a melt, so their different melting points and compositions do not stop the joint.

quiz.q: A brazed gap is d = 0.08 mm. Filler γ = 0.9 N/m, θ = 45°, ρ = 7500 kg/m³. Estimate capillary rise h.
A soldered joint in a car engine bay softens and fails, while a brazed joint nearby survives. Explain.
quiz.a: Solder melts below 450 °C, often at 183–230 °C, so engine-bay heat can soften it; solder also creeps. The braze filler melts above 450 °C and keeps strength at that temperature.

quiz.q: What does flux do in brazing and soldering?
quiz.a: It dissolves oxide and shields the clean metal from air so the filler can wet the surface.

quiz.q: Why are brazed, soldered and adhesive joints usually designed as lap joints rather than butt joints?
quiz.a: The filler or adhesive layer is weaker than the parent metal. A lap joint spreads the load in shear over an overlap area; a butt joint would concentrate load on a thin, weak layer.

quiz.q: Name two heating methods used for brazing.
quiz.a: Torch heating and furnace heating; induction, dip and resistance heating are also used.

beyond: Not for the exam. Vacuum brazing is common for heat exchangers and aerospace parts because no flux residue remains. Lead-free soldering reliability is a large electronics topic; search for intermetallic compound growth and thermal fatigue. Structural adhesives are used in automotive and aircraft assembly, where surface preparation and joint design decide the strength. Good search terms: capillary brazing, reflow soldering profile, lap shear strength of adhesives.
